domains.title: Goddess of War, Invisibility, and the Sun
domains.subtitle: Protector of Warriors and Martial Artists
domains.lead: Marishiten is the Japanese form of Mārīcī, a Buddhist goddess of dawn, light, and victory. In Japan she became a patron of warriors, archers, and practitioners of the martial arts, worshipped for her power to make devotees invisible to harm and irresistible in battle. She rides a boar and is often depicted with multiple arms bearing weapons.

cards.name: Warrior Protector

mythology.lead: Marishiten's mythology is rooted in Indian and Chinese Buddhist texts and adapted in Japan to the needs of warriors.

myths.title: Mārīcī in India
myths.text: In Indian Buddhism, Mārīcī was a goddess of dawn, a ray of light preceding the sun. She was invoked for protection, especially by travelers and those in danger. Her association with invisibility and escape comes from her ability to move unseen before the dawn.

myths.title: Mólìzhītiān
myths.text: Chinese Buddhists translated and depicted Mārīcī as a multi-armed goddess riding a boar or seated in a chariot. She absorbed Taoist solar imagery and became a protector against demons and legal troubles.

myths.title: Patron of Samurai and Archers
myths.text: In Japan, Marishiten became especially popular among samurai and practitioners of kyūdō (archery). Her rituals promised protection from arrows, swords, and harm in battle. Some martial traditions incorporated Marishiten invocations into their secret teachings.

lore.syncretism: Marishiten is a Buddhist warrior goddess who overlaps with Shinto sun kami and Taoist astral figures. Her boar mount connects her to the Japanese zodiac and agricultural cults, while her solar chariot links her to Amaterasu. She represents the Buddhist appropriation of solar and martial power for the protection of the faithful.
lore.culturalLegacy: Marishiten is still venerated in some Buddhist temples and martial arts dojos. Her image appears in Japanese Buddhist iconography, and her name is known to practitioners of traditional archery and swordsmanship. In popular culture she appears as a solar warrior goddess in games and manga.
lore.extendedMeditation: Marishiten teaches that protection can take the form of light. To be invisible to harm is not to hide in darkness but to move in the dawn — seen by the divine, unseen by danger. She is the goddess of those who must face conflict with clarity.

sources.name: Bocking, A Popular Dictionary of Shinto

lore.archaeology: Marishiten is primarily an iconographic and textual figure, preserved in Buddhist statuary, mandalas, and martial-arts manuscripts. Temples such as Hase-dera and Enryaku-ji preserve images of the goddess.
